primary.version: Crash Bandicoot: N. Sane Trilogy on Windows
primary.why: The imported Cash Bandicoot label was corrected to the original Crash Bandicoot, the 1996 PlayStation game, with N. Sane Trilogy as the official modern remaster collection. For a modern archive, Windows N. Sane Trilogy is the highest-fidelity route and includes the first game rebuilt alongside Crash 2 and Warped, with Coco retroactively playable in most levels and official pages listing Stormy Ascent and Future Tense bonus content.
primary.how_to_play: Use Crash Bandicoot: N. Sane Trilogy on Windows for the main capture, with Stormy Ascent installed/available. Keep a short original PlayStation comparison route if the episode needs the 1996 presentation or regional differences, because the remake is a rebuilt modern collection rather than a byte-faithful port.

secondary.exclusive_content: Original 1996 PlayStation presentation and Japanese-release retooling context not reproduced as a byte-faithful port in N. Sane Trilogy.
secondary.what_to_play: Sample the original PlayStation release through DuckStation or original hardware after the Windows remake route, especially any 1996-presentation or Japanese/regional presentation segment.
secondary.why: The PlayStation original had Japanese-release retooling, and N. Sane Trilogy is a rebuilt remaster collection. That makes the original PS1 release a preservation/comparison route, not the main fidelity route.

entries.remaster_caveats: N. Sane Trilogy is a remake collection, not a byte-faithful port. It adds modern visuals, Coco support in most levels, time-trial style modernization across the trilogy, and bonus levels such as Stormy Ascent, but the original PlayStation version should be sampled when discussing original presentation or regional differences.

primary.platform: PocketStation via Japanese PlayStation Crash Bandicoot: Warped
primary.version: Dokodemo Crash / Crash Anywhere downloaded from Crash Bandicoot 3: Buttobi! Sekai Isshuu
primary.why: This is not a normal standalone retail game. The Japanese version of Crash Bandicoot: Warped supports PocketStation, where players can transfer a Crash virtual pet and play minigames; that download is known as Dokodemo Crash, also known as Crash Anywhere. The only honest archive route is the Japanese PlayStation disc plus PocketStation feature path.
primary.how_to_play: Use a Japanese copy of Crash Bandicoot: Warped/Crash Bandicoot 3: Buttobi! Sekai Isshuu with a PocketStation in memory-card slot 1, download Dokodemo Crash, then capture the virtual-pet mode, dancing/rhythm minigames, boulder-run minigame, album/photos, and Warped save-link behavior. Prefer real PocketStation hardware if the episode is about preservation; emulator footage should be labeled only after PocketStation compatibility is verified.

entries.remaster_caveats: No remaster or standalone modern release was sourced. Do not fold this into N. Sane Trilogy coverage; it is a Japanese PocketStation side feature absent from the modern remake route.

primary.why: The Radical Entertainment main version is on PlayStation 2, Wii, Xbox 360, and PSP, with those releases almost identical apart from controls and platform graphics. The Xbox 360 specs include HDTV 720p, 1080i, 1080p, Dolby Digital, and 1-2 player co-op, giving it the highest native-fidelity route for the main game.
primary.how_to_play: Use original Xbox 360 hardware and the Xbox 360 disc/digital release for the primary archive route. Use Xenia only after current build testing; historical loading/save/audio problems have been reported, so emulator capture should not replace hardware without verification.

secondary.exclusive_content: The PSP version is the portable port of the main game and has local Wi-Fi 2-4 player free-for-all / one-on-one multiplayer rather than the console co-op route.
secondary.what_to_play: Only preserve the PSP version if documenting its local wireless multiplayer mode or PSP-specific port behavior.

secondary.exclusive_content: The DS game is an alternate version with a different plot, extensive touchscreen and microphone use, four islands with two levels and a boss each, pachinko boards, Nina sections, and unique enemies, gameplay, and characters compared with other versions.
secondary.what_to_play: Play the full DS campaign separately after the Xbox 360 route, including touchscreen/microphone mechanics, Nina sections, pachinko rewards, collectibles, and alternate ending conditions.

secondary.exclusive_content: The GBA release is a separate 2D side-view action sidescroller with six island locations, co-op support, and its own portable story treatment merging ideas from the DS and console versions.
secondary.what_to_play: Play the GBA campaign for the 2D level layouts and handheld combat route; it is not covered by the Xbox 360 or DS versions.

secondary.exclusive_content: The J2ME version is a side-scrolling beat em up with a Super Mario Bros. 3-style map, automatic attacks while enemies are jacked, totem obstacles, and Wumpa-fruit attack upgrades.
secondary.what_to_play: Archive the mobile route in a J2ME emulator or compatible handset as a distinct short-form phone adaptation.

entries.remaster_caveats: No remaster or modern definitive edition replaces the original releases. Keep the Xbox 360 main route separate from the DS, GBA, J2ME, PSP, and PS2 Monster Edition preservation notes.

entries.title: Crash Party USA

emulation.emulator: BizHawk or another accurate Game Boy Advance emulator

emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Game Boy Advance native 240x160 presentation; emulator scaling is capture-only.

primary.version: Hidden Crash Nitro Kart GBA minigame
primary.why: Crash Party USA is a secret rhythm/dancing minigame on Game Boy Advance, debuting inside the GBA version of Crash Nitro Kart, with dedicated Crash Party USA credits in Crash Nitro Kart GBA. It released on GBA in 2003, accessed via an L/R startup input, with a ten-round reward.
primary.how_to_play: Boot the Game Boy Advance version of Crash Nitro Kart while holding the shoulder-button startup input to enter Crash Party USA, or use the GameCube/GBA link option from Crash Nitro Kart GameCube to play it on a connected GBA. BizHawk has a published TASVideos branch for the Crash Nitro Kart USA minigame route, so GBA emulation is a practical archive path.

secondary.version: Spyro Party USA / Spyro Party reskin in Spyro Orange and Crash Bandicoot Purple
secondary.exclusive_content: Later GBA releases reuse the minigame as Spyro Party USA / Spyro Party with Spyro in place of Crash and localized title screens.
secondary.what_to_play: Play only if preserving the Spyro-reskinned variant; it is not the primary Crash Party USA route.

entries.remaster_caveats: This is not a standalone Crash party game and should not be conflated with Crash Bash or Crash Boom Bang!. Archive it as a hidden GBA minigame tied to Crash Nitro Kart and its later Spyro-reskinned variants.

entries.title: Crash Racing

emulation.emulator: J2ME Loader or KEmulator nnmod
emulation.notes: J2ME Loader and KEmulator nnmod are practical preservation routes for Java ME games. Test multiple known builds/resolutions because preservation listings show several J2ME versions.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original mobile Java handset behavior; emulator scaling is for capture convenience only.

primary.why: Crash Racing is a phone-only Java/J2ME racing game released in December 2005 by Kaolink on J2ME under Vivendi Games Mobile. It is a 2005 mobile game, though some records show it as a 2006 J2ME release in the United States.
primary.how_to_play: Use a preserved JAR/JAD on a compatible Java handset or a J2ME emulator. Match the handset resolution/build when possible because multiple J2ME builds and screen-targeted versions exist.

entries.remaster_caveats: Do not merge this with Crash Tag Team Racing. Crash Racing borrows art, features, characters, and the clashing idea from that console game, but it has its own mobile structure and is a separate J2ME title.

entries.title: Crash Tag Team Racing
entries.definitive_edition: None. The 2007 Crash Bandicoot Action Pack includes the PlayStation 2 version, but it does not supersede the GameCube/Dolphin primary or the PSP linked-content route.

emulation.emulator: Dolphin for primary; PPSSPP/PCSX2 only for secondary link-content preservation
emulation.notes: Dolphin marks the GameCube version Perfect and requires no non-default settings. xemu reports the Xbox version Playable with minor issues, but internal resolution scaling is a known issue; Cxbx-Reloaded historical compatibility reports serious issues.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Dolphin high internal resolution and optional widescreen code for the GameCube build; secondary PSP/PS2 link route should prioritize content access over fidelity.

primary.why: PlayStation 2, GameCube, Xbox, and PSP all received releases. The three home-console versions are mostly identical, with GameCube and Xbox using an unlocked frame rate while PS2 is locked to 30 fps. The GameCube version runs with no reported problems in Dolphin and has 16:9 enhancement codes available, making it the cleanest high-fidelity emulation route for the main game.
primary.how_to_play: Play the GameCube version in Dolphin at a high internal resolution, using the standard controller layout and optional 16:9 Gecko code if the archive capture wants widescreen. Then use the PS2/PSP secondary route for the linked exclusive arenas and cars.

secondary.exclusive_content: The PSP version has two exclusive battle arenas, The Tragic Kingdom and Fight Like an Egyptian, and one exclusive car for each character. The PS2 and PSP versions can unlock each other's alternate goodies via USB, while Xbox and GameCube cannot access that content.
secondary.what_to_play: Use a PSP copy and, if possible, a PS2 copy linked by USB to unlock and play the PSP-exclusive arenas/cars and verify the PS2-side unlocks.

entries.remaster_caveats: Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled later reused some Tag Team Racing characters/content, but it is not a remaster or replacement for Crash Tag Team Racing.

entries.title: Crash Team Racing
entries.definitive_edition: Original PlayStation release via DuckStation or original hardware

emulation.emulator: DuckStation
emulation.notes: Use internal-resolution upscaling only when labeling the footage as enhanced PS1 capture; avoid widescreen or geometry changes for an archival original-route pass.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: PlayStation original rendered above native resolution through PS1 emulation

primary.why: Crash Team Racing is Naughty Dog's 1999 PlayStation kart racer; Nitro-Fueled is a separate 2019 remake. The later PS3/PSP/Vita rows are PlayStation-download access routes, so the original PlayStation release remains the correct primary for this distinct 1999 entry.
primary.how_to_play: Play the NTSC PlayStation version in DuckStation or original hardware. Use high internal resolution only if the episode clearly labels it as enhanced PS1 capture; cover Nitro-Fueled separately as its own remake entry.

entries.remaster_caveats: Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled is a separate 2019 remake with added Nitro Kart and post-launch content. Do not use it as the primary for this original 1999 entry.

entries.title: Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled
entries.definitive_edition: No PC or native next-gen definitive edition was released. The Nitros Oxide Edition is a content bundle/early-unlock package with exclusive cosmetics, not a different technical version.

emulation.emulator: None for primary; use native Xbox hardware/backward compatibility.
emulation.notes: No PC version exists. Use Xbox One X or Series X/S for the primary capture, PS4/PS4 Pro for Retro Stadium and retro cosmetics, and Switch only for portability comparison.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Xbox One X Enhanced / Xbox Series compatibility route at the top console fidelity tier.

primary.version: Xbox One X Enhanced version on Xbox One X or Series X
primary.why: Nitro-Fueled is on PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Nintendo Switch. Both Xbox One X and PS4 Pro run at 2560x1440 and 30fps, but the Xbox version also carries HDR10 and Xbox One X Enhanced support, making it the strongest non-exclusive high-fidelity route. PS4 has exclusive retro content, so it is kept as a secondary content check rather than replacing the Xbox primary.
primary.how_to_play: Use the updated Xbox One version on Xbox One X or Series X for the main Nitro-Fueled route. Then run the PS4 version to capture Retro Stadium plus the PS4-exclusive retro skins/karts if the archive wants every exclusive item.

secondary.why: PS4 has exclusive retro content: retro skins and karts for Crash, Coco, and Cortex, plus a retro track/Retro Stadium. Play this version for that exclusive track and those cosmetics after the primary route.

entries.remaster_caveats: Nitro-Fueled remakes the 1999 Crash Team Racing and adds Crash Nitro Kart/post-launch material, but it should remain separate from the original Crash Team Racing entry. Online features and Wumpa Coin/in-game purchase availability can change.

entries.title: Crash Team Rumble
entries.definitive_edition: No offline or expanded definitive edition was released. After the March 4, 2024 final content update, the core game remained live with a free 500-tier battle pass containing prior seasonal/event rewards, but the experience still depends on online services.

emulation.emulator: None
emulation.notes: Use native Xbox Series X|S or PS5 hardware. Emulation is not practical because the game is online-required and server-dependent.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Native current-gen console release, with Xbox Series X|S selected for the optimized primary route.

primary.why: public release references and Activision list Crash Team Rumble on PS4, PS5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S. It is an online-only 4v4 cross-platform game, and the Xbox listing explicitly marks the title Optimized for Xbox Series X|S with Smart Delivery. No platform-exclusive gameplay content was sourced, so Xbox Series X is the cleanest high-fidelity/current-console route.
primary.how_to_play: Use the Xbox Series X|S version with an Activision account and active console online subscription. Verify server status before capture because the game is online-required and its final content update was March 4, 2024.

entries.remaster_caveats: Not a remaster. It is a live-service-style multiplayer spin-off; final content support ended in 2024 and server availability must be checked before any archive capture.

entries.title: Crash Twinsanity
entries.definitive_edition: No remaster or definitive edition. Crash Bandicoot Action Pack is a three-disc PlayStation 2 bundle containing the PS2 release, not a technically improved version.

emulation.emulator: xemu for the Xbox primary; PCSX2 as a PS2 fallback/comparison route.
emulation.notes: There are currently no known issues running Crash Twinsanity in xemu, but original Xbox emulation should still be play-tested for capture. Xbox 360 backward compatibility is known to be slowdown-prone.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original Xbox 480p progressive/widescreen/Dolby route, captured through native hardware or xemu.

primary.version: Original Xbox release via xemu or original Xbox hardware
primary.why: The console game is on PlayStation 2 and Xbox. The Xbox version supports 480p progressive scan, widescreen, and Dolby Digital, while the PS2 version has widescreen but not progressive scan; PS2 frame-rate problems were also more persistent than Xbox. The Xbox release is therefore the best-fidelity complete console route, with PS2 only needed for comparison or the Action Pack compilation.
primary.how_to_play: Use the Xbox version on original Xbox hardware, or xemu if the current compatibility report still holds. Avoid Xbox 360 backward compatibility for final capture unless specifically testing it, because Xbox 360 backward compatibility has notable slowdowns there.

entries.remaster_caveats: A planned GameCube version was cancelled; do not invent it as a shipped release. The J2ME Crash Twinsanity and Crash Twinsanity 3D mobile games are separate entries with different gameplay.

entries.title: Crash Twinsanity 3D
entries.definitive_edition: No definitive edition or later remaster was found.

emulation.emulator: KEmulator nnmod or J2ME Loader/JL-Mod style tooling
emulation.notes: Use a J2ME emulator that supports 3D APIs. KEmulator nnmod advertises a hardware-accelerated 3D engine and broad OEM API support; J2ME Loader is another useful baseline for many Java ME games.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original J2ME 3D handset rendering, scaled/captured through emulator.

primary.why: Crash Twinsanity 3D is a J2ME release published by Vivendi Games Mobile/Wonderphone and developed by Kuju. It is explicitly not the same as the 2D mobile Crash Twinsanity: this version is a behind-view 3D runner/platformer without the Crash-and-Cortex team-up of the console and 2D mobile games. The release year is dated to 2005; contemporary launch summaries describe a late-2004 Vodafone 3G rollout, so the archive should note the date conflict but keep 2005 as the release-year anchor.
primary.how_to_play: Run the J2ME build in KEmulator nnmod or another J2ME emulator with 3D support, and document the handset/resolution profile used. Test loading and collision-sensitive sections before final capture.

entries.remaster_caveats: Do not confuse this with the console Crash Twinsanity or the 2D J2ME Crash Twinsanity. It has separate behind-view 3D mobile gameplay and no Cortex team-up.

entries.title: Crash Twinsanity Mobile
entries.definitive_edition: No definitive edition or later remaster was found.

emulation.emulator: J2ME Loader or KEmulator nnmod
emulation.notes: J2ME Loader supports most 2D games with per-application settings and scaling; KEmulator is a PC-oriented alternative for Java mobile capture.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Original J2ME 2D handset rendering, scaled/captured through emulator.

primary.why: The mobile Crash Twinsanity is a November 6, 2004 J2ME game published by Wonderphone and developed by Kaolink. Its design is not a port of the full console game: it is a 2D side-view mobile game built around the Doc Amok-style task of protecting Cortex through six levels. No other shipped platform exists.
primary.how_to_play: Use the J2ME build in J2ME Loader or KEmulator, choose the matching handset resolution/profile, and capture all six levels. Keep Crash Twinsanity 3D separate because it is a different mobile game.

entries.remaster_caveats: Do not merge this with the console Crash Twinsanity or Crash Twinsanity 3D. public release references treats the J2ME game as a separate mobile title with different side-view gameplay.
